PROBLEM: Agents calling workflow tools need bounded, revokable authority scoped to their role and work unit; a stolen or stale credential must fail closed without manual revocation.
MECHANISM: Tool leases (src/registry-tool-leases.js): SHA-256-hashed bearer tokens scoped to (project, session, lane) with a role (orchestrator/executor/auditor/dashboard) and an explicit allowedTools subset; validateToolLease checks hash, revocation, expiry, role match, tool grant, and scope match on every call. Sliding renewal (etcd/Consul pattern): a lease used in the second half of its window is pushed to a full window again, max once per half-window, never reviving revoked/expired leases. Refresh credentials (OAuth2 pattern): long-lived (90d idle lapse) credentials that can do exactly one thing — exchange for a lease — and cannot call tools; revoking a credential revokes every lease it issued (credential tree). createToolLease's replaceActiveForActor revokes same-actor/same-scope active leases to prevent duplicate live agents. Lease cap 500 with active-first eviction so volume never 401s a live agent.
INVARIANT: Every agent tool call carries a live, unexpired, unrevoked lease whose role grants the tool and whose scope contains the target work; one live credential per actor+scope.
FAILURE_MODEL: State file holds all lease hashes in plaintext JSON (local disk trust); process death leaves leases valid until expiry (bounded by TTL); clock skew could extend/shorten windows; single local daemon is the only issuer.
SECURITY_MODEL: Token hashes never log plaintext (12-char hash prefix only); tokens returned once at mint; secret redaction on event enqueue; refresh credential != tool lease (validateToolLease rejects credentials); admin-gated bootstrap mint.
SCALING_MODEL: Single-node; 500-lease cap with active-first eviction; leases are small records in state.json; renewals bounded to once per half-window.
CRX_ANALOG: No MCP/tool-execution path exists (audit gap). Ingress-only authorization. CRX has worker runtime but no action-level capability tokens.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca implements ACTION->AUTHORIZATION->EXECUTION->RECEIPT at the tool-call layer with capability leases; CRX has authorization only at mission ingress. The refresh-credential exchange (lapsed lease heals on next exchange) matches CRX's 'bounded retries with evidence' doctrine.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: requires tool-execution path to exist first; lease issuer must be a canonical authority (identity+canonicalization), stored in PG not a second store.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: the exact mechanism class CRX lacks (action-level authorization with receipts, gap #1/#2).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Steal a lease token, expire it, revoke it, swap roles — each must 401/403. Kill the worker mid-lease; the next exchange must self-heal without human action.

PROBLEM: Agents call workflow tools out of order (accept before review, submit before running) or on stale lane state, corrupting lifecycle integrity.
MECHANISM: Workflow state gates (src/registry-tool-leases.js LANE_TOOL_STATE_GATES, enforced by assertAgentToolAllowed): each lifecycle tool is legal only in specific lane states (e.g. lane.submit only in [starting,running]; audit.accept only in [ready_for_audit,auditing,done]). A refused call returns 409 with a computed nextAction envelope pointing at the corrective tool, so the agent can self-correct from the error alone. Flexible ops (stop/retry/controls/evidence) deliberately stay ungated.
INVARIANT: A lifecycle tool call on a lane in a non-listed state is refused, never silently applied; every refusal names the remedy.
FAILURE_MODEL: Gates read lane.state from memory; if state.json was hand-edited, gates follow the lie (state is trusted post-restore). New states must be added to the gate map or tools become unreachable.
SECURITY_MODEL: Enforced server-side; the client cannot grant itself a tool the server did not lease, and cannot bypass the gate map.
SCALING_MODEL: O(1) per call; gate map is static data.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed failure semantics as doctrine but transitions scattered in runtime code; no per-tool legality map against run state.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca turns lifecycle legality into data (tool->allowed-states) with machine-actionable refusals; CRX has the doctrine, not the table. Complements orca-cli/orca O-2 (pure transition table).
INTEGRATION_COST: Very low: a static map + check in the tool-call path once tool execution exists.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: cheap, makes illegal transitions unrepresentable at the agent-tool layer, and gives agents a self-serve recovery path from every refusal.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Attempt audit.accept on a running lane and lane.submit on a queued lane; both must 409 with a nextAction envelope naming a legal tool.

PROBLEM: A spawned agent does not know what to do next: it must poll multiple endpoints and hold the whole workflow model in its prompt, burning context and mis-firing tools.
MECHANISM: Next-action envelope (src/agent-tools/next-action.js): every orchestrator.status (and every refusal) returns a computed envelope: loopState (lane state mapped to a named loop phase), nextRequiredTool (deterministic state machine: no project->register, no session->register, no lane->executor.spawn, queued->observe, running->lane.submit for executors, done->audit.queue_one etc.), nextToolPermitted (whether this role may call it), allowedTools, evidenceRequired/auditRequired/auditSatisfied flags, flow (template, auditTier, fixRouting, maxAuditLoops, loopsRemaining, escalated), capacity (approvedCapacity, activeAgents, idleSlots, spawnPolicy). chooseSessionLane ranks lanes by a priority table (audit.queue_one=30, lane.retry=40, executor.spawn=45, lane.get=50, lane.submit=80, orchestrator.status=90) then recency — the server picks the lane needing attention, not the agent.
INVARIANT: The server always answers 'what should I do next' deterministically from durable state; the agent never needs the workflow model to proceed.
FAILURE_MODEL: If the envelope lies (stale in-memory state), the agent follows it into a 409, which carries a corrected envelope — self-healing. Priority table is static; pathological starvation of low-priority lanes is possible in principle (recency tiebreak mitigates).
SECURITY_MODEL: nextToolPermitted reflects role+lease; the real call still enforces server-side.
SCALING_MODEL: O(lanes) per envelope; the 'lean' variant skips the capability matrix for polled endpoints.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX coordinator context carries this conversationally; nothing machine-readable tells a worker what to do next. Directly addresses campaign §18 (coordinator should do little intelligent work; agents own investigation).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca pushes the scheduling decision INTO the state query (chooseSessionLane+priority), so the agent's only job is to execute the named tool. CRX currently pushes this intelligence into the coordinator's context.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: needs durable task/lane state + a state machine; the envelope shape can be a projection over the PG event journal.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Very high: this is the mechanism that makes workers disposable and the coordinator boring — the envelope survives worker death; any fresh agent can continue from it.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill a worker mid-mission; a brand-new agent with only the envelope endpoint must resume correct sequencing with no coordinator briefing.

PROBLEM: Wakeups (lane finished, audit needed) get lost, duplicated, or delivered to the wrong consumer; a repeat of a still-pending condition should not spam, but a genuinely new occurrence after ack must wake again.
MECHANISM: Durable agent-event queue (src/registry-agent-queue.js): seq-numbered events persisted in state; dedupeKey collapses repeats of a STILL-PENDING condition into occurrences+updatedAt, but an occurrence after a consumer acked is enqueued as a fresh event (fixed bug: acked events used to absorb later occurrences). Drain CONSUMES: event.drain acks what it returns (per-consumer acks keyed role:actor, capped at 64 with keep-key retention). Role-based visibility (orchestrator sees targetRole orchestrator|any; dashboard sees all). Secret redaction on enqueue (key pattern + value pattern). afterSeq/limit/type filters; MAX_AGENT_QUEUE=1000.
INVARIANT: An unacked condition wakes a consumer exactly once per occurrence-batch; a new occurrence after ack is a new wakeup; drain never returns the same backlog twice to the same consumer.
FAILURE_MODEL: Queue lives in state.json (debounced persist); a crash before flush loses the enqueue — the wakeup is lost unless re-enqueued. afterSeq pagination can skip if consumer crashes between pages.
SECURITY_MODEL: Secrets redacted at enqueue; role-gated visibility; acks per consumer so one consumer cannot consume another's wakeup.
SCALING_MODEL: 1000-event cap; acks normalized and capped at 64 per event.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no wakeup queue; subagent results are delivered by the runtime into parent context. Nothing durable survives worker death for re-delivery.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's queue is pull-based durability for agent wakeups with ack semantics; CRX's delivery is push-into-conversation. The dedupe-key-collapse-but-new-after-ack rule is a subtle, correct at-least-once-with-dedupe semantic.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: implement as event-journal-backed outbox with per-consumer ack cursors rather than a separate queue store.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: wakeup durability is required for the interruption experiments (§22) and for missions surviving worker death.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Enqueue audit-required for a lane 3x pre-ack (must collapse to 1 with occurrences=3); ack; enqueue again (must create a NEW event); drain twice (second drain must return empty).

PROBLEM: After a hard daemon restart (SIGKILL), a lane's detached child process group survives with no supervisor — running, burning tokens, holding the worktree — while the persisted lane state says 'running'.
MECHANISM: Interrupted-lane recovery (src/registry-lifecycle.js recoverInterruptedLanes + _reapOrphanedLaneProcess): on boot, for every lane in a state that can hide a live child (not just starting/running — also ready_for_audit/fix_requested/accepted/blocked, since submit sets ready_for_audit without waiting for exit), verify the persisted pid STILL looks like an executor: ps -p <pid> and match the command against a binary pattern derived from the executor table (not hardcoded). PID-REUSE HAZARD handled: a reused pid by an unrelated process is never killed; generic-cli (node) orphans are deliberately left alone rather than risk killing the daemon itself. Reaped->SIGKILL the negative pgid (whole detached group). Then: lanes in starting/running are marked failed ('Controller restarted while lane was active'); lanes that already submitted keep their state (handoff stays auditable) with a log line. Missing ids/paths are repaired with safe defaults.
INVARIANT: No orphaned executor survives a hard restart unverified; a pid is never killed on identity-by-number alone.
FAILURE_MODEL: If ps is unavailable, nothing is reaped (fail-closed toward leaving orphans). Executor binaries renamed after spawn evade the pattern. A lane marked failed may have actually completed its side effects — UNKNOWN_OUTCOME is not reconciled, just recorded.
SECURITY_MODEL: Only the daemon's own executor binaries are killable; negative-pgid kill is scoped to the detached group.
SCALING_MODEL: O(lanes) ps calls at boot, 2s timeout each.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed worker-death failure (WORKER_DEATH) but no boot-time orphan reaping or pid-verification; the §22 interruption experiments will need exactly this.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca treats 'restart' as a recovery event with a typed protocol (verify identity -> reap -> mark failed or preserve handoff). CRX names the failure type but has no reaping mechanism.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: boot-time recovery routine + executor binary registry.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: prerequisite for the coordinator-death experiment; the pid-reuse guard is a reusable invariant for any supervisor.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Start a lane, SIGKILL the daemon, spawn an unrelated process reusing the pid (or simulate), restart: the unrelated process must survive and the lane must be marked failed.

PROBLEM: Frequent state writes (every log line, every event) with naive temp+rename can land OUT of issue order under I/O contention, letting a staler snapshot win the rename race and silently drop fresh state.
MECHANISM: Serialized atomic persistence (src/registry-persistence.js + src/state-store/io.js + recovery.js): persistState() debounces 250ms and bumps an SSE revision counter; _flushPersistTimer snapshots state at flush-ISSUE time and chains the write on _writeChain so the last-issued (freshest) snapshot is the last to hit disk (temp+rename, atomic). readJsonFileWithRecovery: primary->backup->fallback with corrupt-file quarantine (quarantined copy kept, never deleted). Versioned migrations (v1->v3, v2->v3, v3->v4) with byte-preserving backups; a failed migration BLOCKS all further writes (_persistBlocked) rather than overwriting the original. Recovery/migration outcomes are recorded as audit events (registry_state_recovered/registry_state_migrated). Lane journals flush before the snapshot so the snapshot never drops streams the journal failed to write (failed-journal lanes keep streams inline instead).
INVARIANT: The last-issued snapshot is the last to reach disk; a failed migration never overwrites the original; no recovery path silently deletes user state.
FAILURE_MODEL: Single-file state.json: corruption of BOTH primary and backup falls back to empty state (data loss, but announced). Debounce window (250ms) can lose the last writes before a crash.
SECURITY_MODEL: Journal dirs and state files created 0700/0600; corrupt files quarantined, not deleted.
SCALING_MODEL: State file was 525MB before v4 journals (documented in docs/audits/2026-09-10-state-bloat-diagnosis.md); v4 moved streams to per-lane JSONL. Single-node.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has PG journal (stronger durability) but the snapshot-write-ordering hazard and the migration-backup discipline are relevant to any CRX local state (worktree metadata, run ledgers).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's durability is file-local with explicit ordering and recovery semantics; CRX's PG journal is the canonical authority. The harvest is the discipline (write-chain ordering, migration backups, quarantine-not-delete, recovery-as-audit-events), not the store.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: apply to CRX local persistence helpers.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-high: directly applicable to CRX local-state files and to any SQLite/JSONL projections; the 'recovery emits audit events' pattern fits CRX's evidence model.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Crash mid-flush under I/O contention; the recovered state must be the freshest complete snapshot, and both the corrupt original and the backup must be present on disk.

PROBLEM: Self-approval and rubber-stamping: an executor's work is accepted with an empty verdict, or visual work is signed off sight-unseen, or audit->fix loops forever.
MECHANISM: Audit gate (src/registry-audit.js): acceptLaneAudit REFUSES accept unless at least one finding or reviewed file is recorded (current call OR a prior audit.findings.record on the lane) — 409 with a nextAction pointing at audit.findings.record; objects are read for text fields so '[object Object]' cannot satisfy the gate. targetUrl lanes (UI/browser) additionally require captured evidence (screenshot/artifact file in the lane's artifact dir) before accept. Audit loop budget: requestLaneFix counts loops; at maxAuditLoops (default 2, configurable 0-10) the lane ESCALATES to the user instead of looping. Fix routing per flow config: same-agent (lane.retry) or new-agent (executor.spawn). Accept on a still-running lane is refused. Audit queue dedupe: at most ONE pending audit follow-up per lane across both queue event types. Stuck-audit reconciliation (dispatchPendingAudits): lanes in 'auditing' with no live auditor/orchestrator get bounded re-dispatch (MAX_AUDIT_DISPATCHES=2) then escalation — unattended runs cannot hang. Accept triggers guarded worktree reclaim.
INVARIANT: No lane reaches 'accepted' without a recorded human/agent review artifact; no audit loop runs unbounded; no lane hangs in 'auditing' forever.
FAILURE_MODEL: The gate checks recorded text, not review quality — a vacuous finding ('looks good') passes the integrity gate. Auditor and executor are both agents; collusion is not modeled.
SECURITY_MODEL: Accept blocked while a process is live; policy evaluation can require approval for auditLane; audit events are append-only evidence.
SCALING_MODEL: Per-lane audit records capped at 50; findings 100, reviewedFiles 200 per record.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has reviewer-agent and merge-gate concepts in the factory lane but no formal accept-integrity gate, no loop budget, no stuck-verdict reconciliation.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca's gate is evidence-of-review (findings recorded) + budget + escalation; CRX's review vocabulary (from orca-cli O-5) lacks the enforcement. The 'objects cannot rubber-stamp' coercion (auditEntryText) is a real anti-manufactured-success control.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-medium: accept-gate rules + loop counter + escalation state on the review path.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: directly addresses 'CAN A MODEL MANUFACTURE SUCCESS?' — the gate makes empty acceptance structurally impossible.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Call audit.accept with empty findings (must 409); with findings=[{}] (must 409); request fixes 3x (third must escalate, not loop); kill the auditor mid-audit (must re-dispatch then escalate).

PROBLEM: Isolated worktrees accumulate after lanes finish; deleting them carelessly destroys uncommitted or unmerged work.
MECHANISM: Fail-closed worktree reclaim (src/registry-lane-ops.js _reclaimLaneWorktree): removal is allowed ONLY when ALL hold: no live executor process (isLaneProcessLive), git status readable, zero uncommitted changes, branch fully integrated into base (unmerged==0). Every refusal is logged to the lane with the exact reason and the remedy ('Integrate it or discard deliberately; nothing was removed'), recorded on lane.worktreeReclaim. Removal itself is recorded as an audit event with evidence. Triggered on audit.accept and lane.integrate; disabled by ORCA_AUTO_RECLAIM_WORKTREE=false. Branch is kept even when the worktree is removed.
INVARIANT: Anything the system cannot prove redundant is KEPT; every keep names what is unproven and who can resolve it.
FAILURE_MODEL: git status unreadable -> keep (fail-closed). A worktree whose branch was force-pushed elsewhere could be misjudged integrated — mitigated by checking unmerged commits, not just merge-base.
SECURITY_MODEL: Never force-removes; lane.worktree.discard requires explicit force.
SCALING_MODEL: Per-lane git status calls; bounded.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX uses worktrees ad hoc with no create/archive discipline (orca-cli O-3 covers create/archive; this covers the reclaim half).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca pairs creation (O-3) with provably-safe reclamation; the keep-with-reason log is the mechanism that makes cleanup auditable instead of destructive.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: cleanup predicate + audit event on the existing worktree flow.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-high: required for the 50-investigation/10-patch factory scale; prevents the 'who deleted my worktree' failure class.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Accept a lane with uncommitted changes and one with unmerged commits: both worktrees must survive with a logged reason; accept a clean integrated lane: worktree removed, branch kept, audit event present.

PROBLEM: Parallel writer agents corrupt each other's trees; giving every lane its own worktree is wasteful for read-only or sole-writer work.
MECHANISM: Conditional isolation / worktree-on-collision (src/registry-lane-config.js findTreeHolders + describeTreeConflict; AGENTS.md): worktreeMode defaults to 'auto': read-only and sole-writer lanes run DIRECTLY in the project checkout; a dedicated git worktree is created only when writers would collide. Collision predicate: sameExecutionDir equality (not containment — a monorepo root and its app are legitimately parallel) across ALL orchestrators ('a working tree gets exactly one writer across the whole PROJECT, not one per orchestrator'), excluding isolated-by-mode lanes and read-only lanes, using laneOccupiesSlot (a lane that submitted but whose child is still live still holds the tree — state alone under-reports). A refused second writer gets an actionable refusal naming the holder and the three remedies: wait, spawn with worktreeMode 'isolated', or take over the stale orchestrator. Capacity: each orchestrator has approvedCapacity (default 4, max 64); spawning past capacity is REFUSED (409), not queued, with a nextAction.
INVARIANT: One writer per execution directory across the whole project at any time; isolation is created only on proven contention.
FAILURE_MODEL: Equality-not-containment leaves the parent-reaching-into-child residual risk (documented, unchanged policy). Non-git folders degrade 'isolated' to direct silently-ish (documented).
SECURITY_MODEL: The fence bounds where any lane may run; takeover requires the holder to be stale/resigned.
SCALING_MODEL: O(lanes) holder scan per spawn; capacity default 4/orchestrator.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX uses worktrees ad hoc; no collision predicate; no per-orchestrator capacity. Campaign §18: the coordinator owns capability bounds — this is the mechanism.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca derives isolation from OBSERVED contention (holder scan) rather than policy-always-isolate; CRX currently has neither the predicate nor the capacity refusal.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-medium: holder-scan predicate + capacity field on the worker-spawn path.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: enables safe parallel patch workers without paying a worktree per lane; the refuse-not-queue capacity rule prevents silent queue growth.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Two orchestrators spawn writers on the same checkout: the second must 409 naming the first; a read-only lane on the same checkout must be allowed; spawning a 5th lane at capacity 4 must 409, not queue.

PROBLEM: Lane logs and agent events ballooned state.json to 525MB (199MB streams); every persist rewrote them and every restart re-read them.
MECHANISM: Per-lane journals (src/lane-journal.js): logs and agent events live in append-only JSONL segment files under lanes/<lane>/ (8MB segments, 4 hot segments, older rotated to archive/ — nothing dropped). Appends are crash-tolerant: a torn final line (crash mid-append) is skipped, never fatal; appends start on a fresh line so torn bytes cannot swallow the new entry. Readers take bounded tails reading backwards in 64KB chunks through rotated+archived segments only as far as needed. Snapshot drops streams from state.json but journals FIRST, and a lane whose journal append failed keeps streams inline instead. __proto__/constructor/prototype reviver guard on parse.
INVARIANT: Hot state stays small; every log line is preserved somewhere; a torn write never corrupts subsequent reads.
FAILURE_MODEL: Disk-full during append loses the tail of that write (detected: journal-first ordering keeps it inline). Archive dir unbounded over long retention (state-gc lane handles).
SECURITY_MODEL: Journal dirs 0700, files 0600; prototype-pollution guard on parse.
SCALING_MODEL: Bounded hot segments; tail reads O(requested lines), not O(file).
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has PG journal (better) but per-run evidence bundles (orca-cli O-8) and JSONL run ledgers could use the journal discipline.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Separation of hot queryable state from append-only evidence streams, with rotation/archival and torn-write tolerance.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: adopt for file-based run ledgers.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: pattern for CRX per-run evidence bundles at factory scale.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill mid-append; the next read must skip exactly the torn line. Grow a lane past 4 segments; the 5th must rotate to archive with nothing lost.

PROBLEM: Audit events embedded live lane objects: in memory the 'evidence' mutated with the lane; on disk every event re-serialized the whole lane (300MB of a 525MB state file). Result text silently truncated at 12,000 chars lost 58% of a real 28,719-char report (2026-09-11 incident).
MECHANISM: Evidence-by-reference (src/audit-evidence.js) + honest truncation (src/lane-result.js): an audit event records which lane, the state AT the event, and a sha256 digest of the canonical lane record (streams excluded, keys sorted — stable across live/restored/archived copies). The full record stays in the lane. Lane results: full text ALWAYS written to the lane's result.txt artifact; what is stored is capped at 32,000 chars (sized from measured medians) with a notice giving full length and naming the artifact; structured fields resultTruncated/resultFullLength/resultArtifact travel with it; a 1MB runaway capture ceiling prevents unbounded copy. Previews append a one-line warning so clipped results never read as complete.
INVARIANT: Evidence never mutates after the event; a stored result either is complete or says exactly how much is missing and where the rest lives.
FAILURE_MODEL: Digest covers the record minus streams; stream content is referenced by journal path, not hashed. Artifact deletion breaks the reference (detectable: digest of record vs missing artifact).
SECURITY_MODEL: Digests are tamper-evident for the record; no secrets in evidence (secret redaction at enqueue).
SCALING_MODEL: Evidence records are small and fixed-schema; results bounded.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's evidence authority and canonical journal already separate source truth from derived truth; this is the same principle with a concrete digest+artifact discipline CRX lacks for large worker outputs.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca learned from a real truncation incident and now treats 'stored preview vs complete artifact' as a first-class distinction with machine-readable fields. CRX should adopt the discipline for worker result capture.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: result-capture wrapper + digest function on worker outputs.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-high: prevents the manufactured-completeness failure (a clipped result reading as whole) and keeps evidence stores small.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Submit a 100KB report; stored text must end with the truncation notice, result.txt must hold all 100KB byte-identical, and the digest must verify against the lane record.

PROBLEM: Two daemons over one state directory destroy each other: startup restores, migrates, and SIGKILLs process groups a persisted lane still points at — a duplicate would kill the live daemon's workers.
MECHANISM: Instance lock with machine identity (src/instance-lock.js + src/machine-identity.js): O_EXCL-created daemon.lock records pid AND the pid's kernel start time (ps -o lstart, TZ/LC pinned) AND a stable machine identity (macOS platform UUID, /etc/machine-id, else UUID file) — never hostname (documented incident: hostname changes stranded a live daemon). A lock is stale only when the owner is provably gone on THIS machine; anything unverifiable counts as HELD (a refused start is recoverable, a second daemon on live state is not). Takeover only after proof; --force is explicit break-glass that still refuses when the pid cannot be checked at all.
INVARIANT: At most one live owner per state directory; identity is (machine, pid, pid-start-time), never pid alone, never hostname.
FAILURE_MODEL: Network filesystems weaken O_EXCL; a machine-identity collision (cloned VM image) could allow dual ownership — documented residual.
SECURITY_MODEL: The lock module never signals any process; takeover is explicit and audited.
SCALING_MODEL: Single state dir per machine; no cross-machine story.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX coordinator runs are conversational; no singleton enforcement on shared state. Relevant if CRX ever runs a daemon coordinator over shared ledgers.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Identity-by-(machine,pid,start-time) is the correct primitive; CRX currently has no equivalent.
INTEGRATION_COST: Very low: ~100 lines, no dependencies.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: directly reusable if CRX builds a persistent coordinator; the pid-start-time trick is a standalone pattern.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Start two daemons on one state dir: the second must exit 1 naming the owner, changing nothing. Reuse the pid with an unrelated process: takeover must be refused.

PROBLEM: Agents must not roam the filesystem; a misconfigured daemon should not silently grant the whole machine.
MECHANISM: The fence (src/fence.js): exact root list; the daemon's working directory is never added; no roots is a named state (setup-required), never a default; home-covering roots require a recorded acknowledgement (--allow-home-root); home resolved from the user database (os.userInfo), not $HOME, so an overridden HOME cannot disguise a whole-home root. Every surface that reports the fence names the one fix command. Agents cannot change the fence — only an operator on the workstation can. Malformed roots are INVALID (refuse everything), not ignored.
INVARIANT: No agent registers and no executor launches outside the fence; misconfiguration fails closed to 'registers nothing'.
FAILURE_MODEL: Symlink races: roots are resolved to real paths at config time; a root later replaced by a symlink to elsewhere is not re-resolved per call (residual).
SECURITY_MODEL: Fail-closed; acknowledgement recorded for home-wide roots; operator-only mutation.
SCALING_MODEL: O(roots) per check; trivial.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX workers run with the agent's ambient filesystem access; no explicit work-boundary primitive.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca makes the work boundary explicit data (roots) with named states; CRX relies on the runtime sandbox implicitly.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: root list + check on worker spawn.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: cheap boundary primitive for disposable workers; complements worktree isolation.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Set ORCA_REPO_ROOTS to a nonexistent dir: all spawns must 409. Override HOME to narrow a home-covering root: must still be flagged home-wide.

PROBLEM: A Claude Code orchestrator is only woken by its own tool output: a completed lane enqueues a durable wakeup event, but nothing delivers it — the orchestrator discovers the finish only when asked (real incident: lane finished 17:01, found out much later).
MECHANISM: Lane-state watcher (src/cli-watch.js, wired by commits bb416e6 + 5b339e8): markLaneCompleted/Failed/Stopped enqueue a durable wakeup event; the watcher CLI polls the non-mutating lane.list route and prints exactly one line per real lane state change ('<laneId8> <title> <from>→<to>'), silent otherwise, one line on daemon outage and one on reconnect, no tokens in output, exits when no active lane remains (--forever to persist). It is meant to run under a Monitor-style streaming-output tool so each printed line becomes tool output that wakes the session. orchestrator.register and executor.spawn return the exact ready-to-run watch command in a `watch` field; role instructions tell every registering orchestrator to start it after the first spawn.
INVARIANT: Every terminal lane transition is observable as a single line of tool output by the orchestrator that spawned it; the orchestrator never has to compose the watch command.
FAILURE_MODEL: Polling (default interval) not push: latency bounded by interval; a watcher killed silently stops wakeups (the durable queue still holds them).
SECURITY_MODEL: Uses the non-mutating route; no tokens in output; lease-scoped.
SCALING_MODEL: One poll per interval per orchestrator; lane.list is a read projection.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX subagent results are delivered automatically by the runtime into parent context — push, not pull. But for any future daemon-mode coordinator (persistent, outside a chat), the wakeup problem is real and unsolved.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Orca acknowledges the pull/push mismatch explicitly and ships a dedicated watcher rather than pretending the queue is enough. The 'return the exact command in the spawn response' wiring is a nice contract touch.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low for the pattern; the CLI itself is Orca-specific.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: the pattern (terminal-transition wakeups + exact-command handoff) applies to any CRX persistent-coordinator design; the polling implementation is a stopgap.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Complete a lane while the orchestrator idles: the watcher must print exactly one line for the transition and nothing else; kill the watcher: the event must still be drainable from the queue.

PROBLEM: A crash or restart in the middle of a multi-step graph run loses partial progress, and re-running from scratch wastes compute and can double-apply side effects.
MECHANISM: Pregel superstep execution with checkpointed channel state. In each superstep, tasks write to named channels; _algo.py groups writes by channel, applies them, and bumps per-channel versions in the checkpoint dict (checkpoint['channel_versions']). The checkpointer persists the checkpoint after every superstep, so a run can resume from any checkpoint id (time travel). Source: libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py, libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py.
INVARIANT: Channel versions only advance when writes are successfully applied; re-loading a checkpoint and replaying its writes is idempotent with respect to channel state.
FAILURE_MODEL: A checkpointer write failure aborts the step. A crash mid-superstep re-executes that superstep's tasks from the last good checkpoint, so non-idempotent nodes can double-apply effects. Exactly-once is not guaranteed for task bodies.
SECURITY_MODEL: The checkpointer is pluggable storage with no built-in auth or encryption; whoever holds the thread_id can read and fork the checkpoint.
SCALING_MODEL: Runs partition by thread_id; checkpoint size grows with channel state, so large shared state makes every superstep write heavier.
CRX_ANALOG: MissionRuntime deterministic mission ids plus the canonical ping_events log. CRX has append-only facts but no mutable per-superstep state snapshot.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: LangGraph checkpoints are mutable state snapshots with version vectors keyed by channel; CRX events are immutable facts. LangGraph answers 'what is the state now', CRX answers 'what happened'.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: would require a checkpoint-shaped projection over ping_events plus a thread/run identity CRX currently lacks (known gap: no durable per-attempt Run identity).
EXPECTED_VALUE: High for long missions: resume-from-checkpoint and time-travel debugging directly address CRX's missing run-identity and recovery story.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Kill the process mid-run, reload the thread from the last checkpoint id, and resume; assert the run continues without re-executing already-checkpointed supersteps and that channel_versions in the stored checkpoint strictly increase.

PROBLEM: Long autonomous runs need a human decision at a specific point without losing the run: pausing must be durable and resumable at exactly the paused node.
MECHANISM: A node calls interrupt(value); the Interrupt carries a deterministic id derived as xxh3_128 of the checkpoint namespace path (Interrupt.from_ns), the run halts, and the checkpoint is persisted. The caller resumes with Command(resume=<value>), which routes the response back to the exact paused interrupt. Source: libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py (Interrupt class, from_ns, id), pregel/_loop.py.
INVARIANT: The interrupt id is a pure function of the namespace path, so a resume token unambiguously identifies which pause point it answers, even across restarts.
FAILURE_MODEL: An interrupt that is never resumed leaves the thread parked forever; the interrupt value must be serializable by the checkpointer or the pause itself fails.
SECURITY_MODEL: Anyone who can submit a Command(resume=...) to the thread can answer the interrupt; there is no per-interrupt authorization.
SCALING_MODEL: Parked threads hold one checkpoint each; resume is O(1) lookup by thread id.
CRX_ANALOG: No analog. CRX has no pause/resume primitive and no human-approval gate in the mission runtime (known gap: no action-level authorization beyond ingress).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Interrupt is a first-class control-flow primitive persisted in the checkpoint stream; CRX would need a new event type plus a parked-run state to represent it.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: needs a parked-run state in MissionRuntime, a resume command path, and deterministic pause-point ids. The xxh3-from-namespace trick ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: this is the cleanest known shape for human-in-the-loop approval gates, which CRX needs for high-stakes tool actions.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Raise interrupt() inside a node, terminate the process, restart, and resume with Command(resume=...); assert execution continues inside the same node with the supplied value and that two sibling interrupts produce distinct ids.

PROBLEM: Transient node failures (rate limits, flaky tools) should be retried with backoff without failing the whole run or writing custom retry loops in every node.
MECHANISM: RetryPolicy NamedTuple on a node: initial_interval, backoff_factor, max_interval, max_attempts, jitter, and retry_on (exception classes or predicate). The executor retries only matching failures with exponential backoff plus jitter. Source: libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py (class RetryPolicy).
INVARIANT: Only exceptions matching retry_on trigger a retry, and total attempts never exceed max_attempts including the first try.
FAILURE_MODEL: Exhaustion surfaces the last error into the checkpoint; retried nodes that are not idempotent can double-apply side effects between attempts.
SECURITY_MODEL: No security boundary; retry policy is configuration, not authorization.
SCALING_MODEL: Retries are local to the node task; backoff sleeps hold a worker slot for the duration.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed failure semantics in WorkerRuntime but no declarative per-step retry policy with backoff and jitter.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: RetryPolicy is declarative config attached to the work definition; CRX failure handling is currently imperative in the runtime.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: a retry policy struct on mission steps plus executor support for backoff/jitter; the retry_on predicate shape ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: removes a class of ad-hoc retry code and makes retry budgets auditable per step.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Configure max_attempts=3 with a node that always raises a matching exception; assert exactly 3 attempts, increasing delays, and that a non-matching exception fails on attempt 1.

PROBLEM: Static graph edges cannot express fan-out where the number of parallel tasks is only known at runtime (map over a dynamic list).
MECHANISM: Send targets a node with a runtime-constructed payload, spawning one task instance per Send; Command lets a node update shared state and route to the next node(s). Together they give dynamic map-reduce inside a statically defined graph. Source: libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py (Send, Command), libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py, libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py.
INVARIANT: Each Send creates a distinct task with its own id; tasks spawned in one superstep run in the next superstep, preserving the bulk-synchronous barrier.
FAILURE_MODEL: Unbounded Send fan-out can exhaust the executor; a failing Send target fails the superstep and is checkpointed as a task error.
SECURITY_MODEL: No capability restriction on which nodes a Send can target; routing is trusted.
SCALING_MODEL: Fan-out parallelism is bounded by the executor's max concurrency; checkpoint size grows with the number of spawned tasks.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX WorkerRuntime results reify as canonical events but CRX has no dynamic fan-out primitive; parallel work is arranged ad hoc by the parent agent.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Send is runtime-planned parallelism inside a declarative graph; CRX parallelism is orchestrator-planned outside the runtime.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium-high: needs a task-spawn event type, per-spawn ids, and a barrier semantic in MissionRuntime.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: useful for map-style missions (e.g. fan out over N prospects), but only pays off once CRX has run identity and checkpointing.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Emit N Sends from one node with N only known at runtime; assert N distinct task ids execute in the following superstep and all complete before the downstream node runs.

PROBLEM: Multi-agent runs need stopping rules that combine several conditions (max turns AND a stop phrase AND a timeout), but hardcoded stop logic is not reusable or inspectable.
MECHANISM: Termination conditions as composable objects: StopMessageTermination, MaxMessageTermination, TextMentionTermination, FunctionalTermination, TokenUsageTermination, HandoffTermination, TimeoutTermination, ExternalTermination, SourceMatchTermination, TextMessageTermination, FunctionCallTermination, combined with & and | operators defined on TerminationCondition. Checked after every message. Source: python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/conditions/_terminations.py, base/_termination.py.
INVARIANT: Termination is evaluated after each message against the full thread; composed conditions evaluate deterministically left to right with short-circuit.
FAILURE_MODEL: A raising predicate inside FunctionalTermination propagates and can kill the run instead of stopping it cleanly; with no termination condition a team runs unbounded.
SECURITY_MODEL: ExternalTermination lets outside code stop a run, which is a control input that must itself be authorized by the host.
SCALING_MODEL: O(conditions) checks per message; negligible cost next to model calls.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX missions have no declarative stop conditions; stopping is orchestrator judgment plus the disposable-subagent pattern.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: AutoGen termination is a data structure over the message thread; CRX stop decisions live in the orchestrator's head, not in the mission record.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: a termination-condition type evaluated by MissionRuntime after each worker result event; the & / | composition ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: makes 'when is this mission done' explicit, auditable, and reusable instead of vibes-based.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Compose MaxMessageTermination(5) | TextMentionTermination('DONE'); run a team that says DONE on message 3 and assert the run stops at 3, and run one that never says it and assert it stops at exactly 5.

PROBLEM: Agents and teams must be pausable and migratable, but their state (LLM context, turn counters, speaker pointers) is scattered across live objects.
MECHANISM: Every agent and team implements save_state/load_state over typed pydantic snapshots: BaseState carries type and version fields, AssistantAgentState holds llm_context, TeamState aggregates agent_states, and group-chat managers persist message_thread, current_turn, and speaker pointers (e.g. RoundRobinManagerState.next_speaker_index). Source: python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/state/_states.py, teams/_group_chat/_base_group_chat.py.
INVARIANT: A saved snapshot plus the same code version reconstructs an equivalent agent; version field allows migration shims.
FAILURE_MODEL: The runtime does NOT persist snapshots durably; save_state returns a dict and the caller must store it. A crash between save_state and the caller's write loses the state. Loading a snapshot into a different agent topology silently misbehaves.
SECURITY_MODEL: Snapshots contain full message history including tool outputs; whoever holds a snapshot holds the conversation.
SCALING_MODEL: Snapshot size grows with message_thread; per-agent states are independent and can be stored separately.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no memory retrieval in execution and no agent state snapshots (known gaps); WorkerRuntime results reify as events but intermediate agent state does not.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: AutoGen state is an explicit serializable object with schema versioning; CRX would have to derive it from the event log or add a snapshot table.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: define snapshot schemas per runtime component and a durable snapshot store; the type+version envelope ports directly. Durability must be added (AutoGen leaves it to the caller).
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: pausable/migratable agents are prerequisite for long autonomous missions that survive restarts.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: save_state mid-run, terminate the process, load_state into a fresh team, and continue; assert the next speaker and turn counter match the pre-save values. Then delete the caller's stored snapshot and confirm the runtime alone cannot recover.

PROBLEM: In a team of specialists, the next worker should be chosen by the current worker's explicit delegation, not by a central scheduler that must understand every task.
MECHANISM: HandoffMessage carries an explicit target participant name; the Swarm manager routes solely on handoff messages, and HandoffTermination ends a run when a handoff to a terminal target occurs. Invalid targets fail loudly at resume/startup validation. Source: python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/teams/_group_chat/_swarm_group_chat.py, conditions/_terminations.py, messages.py.
INVARIANT: Every handoff target must name a valid participant; a handoff to an unknown name raises instead of silently dropping the task.
FAILURE_MODEL: An agent that never emits a handoff stalls the swarm; two agents handing off to each other loop until a termination condition fires.
SECURITY_MODEL: Any participant can hand off to any other; there is no per-agent delegation allowlist.
SCALING_MODEL: Routing is O(1) per handoff; the thread is the shared state.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX subagents are disposable and orchestrator-assigned; there is no agent-to-agent delegation primitive.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Handoff is worker-initiated routing; CRX routing is orchestrator-initiated. Handoff moves scheduling knowledge into the workers.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: needs a delegation event type and a routing rule in MissionRuntime; the target-validation invariant ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: reduces orchestrator bottleneck for specialist chains, but needs termination conditions (AG-01) to be safe.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run a swarm where agent A hands off to a nonexistent agent B; assert the run raises a validation error rather than stalling, and assert a valid A->B handoff delivers the message to B next.

PROBLEM: Sequential tasks need the outputs of earlier tasks as input, but passing outputs through the orchestrator by hand is fragile and loses the dependency structure.
MECHANISM: Task.context is a list of Task objects whose outputs are injected as context when the dependent task executes. Dependencies are declared as data (task references), not as orchestration code. Source: lib/crewai/src/crewai/task.py (field 'context').
INVARIANT: A task does not execute until every task in its context list has produced an output.
FAILURE_MODEL: A failed context task propagates failure or stale output downstream; cyclic context references are not statically rejected and can deadlock.
SECURITY_MODEL: Task outputs flow to dependents without redaction; sensitive tool output in an upstream task leaks into every downstream prompt.
SCALING_MODEL: Context injection grows the downstream prompt linearly with upstream outputs; no streaming or reference-passing.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX worker results reify as canonical events, but wiring one worker's output into another's input is done ad hoc by the parent agent, not declared.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: CrewAI dependencies are declared edges between work items; CRX dependencies are implicit in orchestrator prompts.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: declare input edges on mission steps referencing prior step outputs; the runtime resolves them from the event log.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: makes data flow between steps explicit and auditable, which CRX's event log already supports well.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Declare task B with context=[A] where A fails; assert B never executes, and declare a cyclic A<->B pair and observe the documented behavior (deadlock or error).

PROBLEM: For open-ended goals, the decomposition itself is the hard part; a static task list cannot adapt when subtasks turn out wrong.
MECHANISM: Hierarchical process: a manager agent (or manager LLM) receives the goal, decomposes it, delegates subtasks to worker agents, and synthesizes results. Requires manager_llm or manager_agent to be set; the manager plans and assigns rather than executing a fixed list. Source: lib/crewai/src/crewai/crew.py, process.py.
INVARIANT: Hierarchical crews refuse to run without an explicit manager (validation error), so delegation authority is never implicit.
FAILURE_MODEL: A weak manager produces poor decompositions and there is no built-in verification of the plan; delegation loops are possible if the manager re-delegates to itself.
SECURITY_MODEL: The manager inherits the union of worker tool permissions; a compromised manager has full crew authority.
SCALING_MODEL: One manager is the bottleneck; worker parallelism is bounded by the manager's ability to specify independent subtasks.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX's parent agent already acts as a delegating manager over disposable subagents; this formalizes that pattern.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: CrewAI makes the manager a typed crew role with validation; CRX's manager is an emergent behavior of the main agent, not a runtime construct.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low if kept as a pattern; medium to make the manager role explicit in MissionRuntime with delegation events.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Low-medium as a mechanism (CRX already does this); the value is the validation invariant: refuse to run a hierarchical crew with no manager.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Construct a hierarchical crew with no manager_llm and no manager_agent; assert it raises a validation error before any worker runs.

PROBLEM: Agent trajectories are usually opaque blobs; debugging, replay, and cost accounting need structured per-step records.
MECHANISM: Every run appends typed step dataclasses to AgentMemory: TaskStep, ActionStep (step_number, timing, model_input_messages, tool_calls, error, observations, action_output, token_usage), PlanningStep (plan, timing, token_usage), FinalAnswerStep. Each step serializes to a dict and can be converted back to messages, making trajectories replayable and auditable. Source: src/smolagents/memory.py.
INVARIANT: Steps are appended in execution order with monotonically increasing step_number; every step carries timing and optional token usage.
FAILURE_MODEL: Steps live in memory; a crash loses the trajectory unless the caller persists step dicts. Serialization of arbitrary action_output can fail.
SECURITY_MODEL: Step records contain full model inputs including tool results; persisting them persists secrets that appeared in observations.
SCALING_MODEL: Memory grows linearly with steps; to_messages(summary_mode=True) gives a cheap projection.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed failure semantics and event reification but no per-step typed trajectory; observability tables are empty (known gap).
SEMANTIC_DELTA: smolagents steps are structured run records, not log lines; they are designed to be replayed into messages, which is exactly CRX's projection idea applied to trajectories.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-medium: define step event types in ping_events; the per-step field set (timing, token usage, tool calls, error, observations) ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: fills CRX's empty observability story with a concrete, replayable step schema.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run an agent, serialize memory.steps to dicts, rebuild a new AgentMemory from them, and assert to_messages() reproduces the original trajectory; then kill the process mid-run and confirm the in-memory steps are gone.

PROBLEM: A manager agent needs to call specialist subagents, but giving the manager raw subprocess control is untyped and unobservable.
MECHANISM: Managed agents are registered on the manager and exposed to the model as tools: each managed agent gets a fixed schema with a single 'task' string input and an 'additional_args' object for extra context (images, dataframes). The manager invokes a subagent exactly like a tool call, so delegation is visible in the tool_calls of the ActionStep. Source: src/smolagents/agents.py (_setup_managed_agents).
INVARIANT: Every managed agent must have a name and description (asserted at setup), and its tool schema is fixed to task+additional_args regardless of the subagent's internals.
FAILURE_MODEL: The subagent's full trajectory is hidden behind the tool-call boundary; only its returned string is visible to the manager, so debugging delegation failures requires the subagent's own memory.
SECURITY_MODEL: The managed agent runs with its own tools and permissions; the manager cannot see or constrain the subagent's tool use beyond the task string.
SCALING_MODEL: Delegation is synchronous from the manager's perspective; nested delegation depth is bounded only by max_steps.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX disposable subagents without transcript inheritance are the same idea; smolagents formalizes the boundary as a tool schema.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: The subagent-as-tool boundary is explicit and typed here; CRX's subagent boundary is a runtime convention.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: document the subagent invocation as a typed tool call in the mission record; the fixed task+additional_args schema ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: makes delegation boundaries observable in the trajectory, which helps CRX's verification story.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Register a managed agent without a name; assert setup raises. Invoke it and assert the manager's ActionStep records a tool call whose output is exactly the subagent's final string.

PROBLEM: The agent's context (LLM messages) and the system's record of what happened drift apart: retries, condensation, and UI edits create two truths.
MECHANISM: All activity appends to an immutable event log of frozen pydantic Event objects (frozen=True, extra='forbid', with EventID, timestamp, source). LLM messages are a derived projection: events_to_messages() converts LLMConvertibleEvents to messages, merging and combining as needed. The log is the source of truth; messages are computed. Source: openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/base.py.
INVARIANT: Events are immutable once appended; message history is always recomputable from the log, so the model-visible context can never diverge from the record.
FAILURE_MODEL: A bug in events_to_messages can show the model a misleading projection while the log stays correct; consumers that bypass the log and cache messages reintroduce drift.
SECURITY_MODEL: Frozen models prevent in-place tampering, but anyone with write access to the log store can append misleading events; the log needs append-only enforcement at the store layer.
SCALING_MODEL: Log grows linearly with activity; message derivation is O(events) per turn unless cached.
CRX_ANALOG: Direct analog to CRX/PING's event sourcing: ping_events is canonical, projections are derived. OpenHands independently converged on the same layering.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Nearly identical semantics; the delta is enforcement: frozen pydantic models at the type level plus a single named projection function, where CRX relies on convention plus fail-closed canonicalization.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: adopt the frozen-event + single-projection-function discipline in CRX's event definitions; no new infrastructure.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: independent production-grade validation of CRX's core architectural bet, plus a concrete enforcement pattern (frozen models, one projection function) CRX can copy.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Append events, derive messages, then attempt to mutate an event in place; assert the mutation raises (frozen). Derive messages twice and assert identical output.

PROBLEM: Tool calls with irreversible effects (deleting files, running untrusted code) need a risk judgment before execution, but static allowlists cannot judge novel commands.
MECHANISM: Every ActionEvent carries a security_risk field of type SecurityRisk (UNKNOWN/LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH) predicted by an LLM risk analyzer at action time, plus the agent's thought. HIGH risk triggers a human confirmation gate before execution. Source: openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/llm_convertible/action.py, security/risk.py.
INVARIANT: The risk label is stored on the action event itself, so the risk judgment is part of the permanent record and auditable after the fact.
FAILURE_MODEL: The risk score is a model prediction, not a proof: it can under-rate a dangerous action (false LOW) or over-rate a safe one (false HIGH causing confirmation fatigue). Analyzer outage must fail closed to HIGH/UNKNOWN.
SECURITY_MODEL: The analyzer is itself an LLM call that sees the action; prompt-injected tool arguments could try to influence the risk narrative, so the risk field must never be settable by the agent.
SCALING_MODEL: One extra LLM call per action; can be batched or cached for repeated identical actions.
CRX_ANALOG: No analog; CRX has no action-level authorization beyond ingress (known gap). This is the closest production shape to what CRX needs.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Risk is a graded prediction stored on the action, not a binary allow/deny; CRX currently has no per-action judgment at all.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: add a risk field to tool-execution events, an analyzer step before effectful tools, and a confirmation gate for HIGH. The enum and on-event storage port directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: fills CRX's biggest known authorization gap with a production-tested pattern, including the auditability property.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Submit a file-deletion action and a read-only action; assert the risk labels differ and HIGH blocks without confirmation. Attempt to set security_risk from agent-controlled input and assert it is ignored or overwritten by the analyzer.

PROBLEM: Long runs blow the context window, but summarizing by rewriting history destroys the audit trail and breaks replay.
MECHANISM: Condensation is itself an event: when the log exceeds a threshold, an LLM summarizes the middle (keeping the first events pinned via keep_first and recent events intact) and a CondensationSummaryEvent is appended to the log at the position where the summarized span was. History is never rewritten; consumers that want the compact view skip the summarized span. Source: openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/condenser.py.
INVARIANT: Only new events are appended; no existing event is ever mutated or deleted by condensation, so full-fidelity replay remains possible.
FAILURE_MODEL: A bad summary loses information for consumers using the compact view; the full log is still intact, so recovery is re-derivation, not data loss.
SECURITY_MODEL: The summarizer LLM sees the full span; secrets in the summarized region persist in the summary unless the summarizer is instructed to redact.
SCALING_MODEL: Condensation cost is one LLM call per threshold crossing; compact-view derivation skips the summarized span in O(1).
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no forgetting path (known gap). This is the safe shape for one: forget by summarizing, never by deleting.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Condensation-as-event preserves CRX's append-only invariant while adding bounded context; naive truncation would violate it.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: define a condensation event type in ping_events, a summarizer step, and projection rules that skip summarized spans. The keep_first pinning rule ports directly.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: gives CRX the missing forgetting path without breaking event-sourcing guarantees.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run condensation over a long log; assert every pre-existing event is byte-identical afterwards, that a CondensationSummaryEvent exists, and that the compact projection is shorter while the full projection is unchanged.

PROBLEM: Raw trajectories contain huge tool outputs that drown the model's context; every harness hand-rolls truncation logic tangled into the agent loop.
MECHANISM: History processing is a pluggable pipeline stage: AbstractHistoryProcessor takes the full History and returns a transformed History before the model sees it. Provided processors include DefaultHistoryProcessor and LastNObservations (keep only the last N observations, eliding older ones). Source: sweagent/agent/history_processors.py.
INVARIANT: The stored trajectory is never modified; the processor only transforms the model-visible view, so the audit record keeps full fidelity.
FAILURE_MODEL: An aggressive processor can elide the observation containing the key error, causing the model to loop; the full history is still available for a fallback processor.
SECURITY_MODEL: Processors see full history including secrets in tool output; a processor could exfiltrate, so processors are trusted code.
SCALING_MODEL: Processing is O(history) per step; LastNObservations keeps prompt size bounded regardless of run length.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no memory retrieval in execution and no context-shaping stage (known gaps); the full event log would be the model input without one.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: The processor is an explicit, swappable pipeline stage between stored truth and model view; CRX currently has no such stage.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low-medium: define a history-processor interface over the event projection; LastNObservations ports directly as a first processor.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium-high: prerequisite for long missions; separates what happened (full log) from what the model sees (bounded view).
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run a trajectory with a huge early observation; assert the stored trajectory still contains it while the model-visible history does not, and swap in a pass-through processor to confirm the model then sees everything.

PROBLEM: A single attempt at a hard task often fails; blind retries waste compute, but giving up after one try wastes the work. Retries need judgment about which attempt was best.
MECHANISM: RetryAgent wraps the worker with a reviewer loop: each attempt runs to completion, a reviewer scores or chooses among submissions (ScoreRetryLoop / ChooserRetryLoop producing ReviewerResult), per-attempt InstanceStats accumulate, and the trajectory is saved per problem id (<id>.traj). Config is deep-copied per instance to avoid shared state. Source: sweagent/agent/agents.py (RetryAgent), reviewer.py.
INVARIANT: Attempt stats are per-instance and never shared between problem instances (deep-copied config); the reviewer sees submissions, not internal agent state.
FAILURE_MODEL: The reviewer is itself fallible and can pick a worse attempt; unbounded retries need an external attempt cap or the loop burns budget.
SECURITY_MODEL: Reviewer prompts include the submission content; a malicious submission could try to influence the reviewer, so reviewer and worker should be separated.
SCALING_MODEL: Attempts are sequential; cost multiplies by the number of attempts.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has typed failure semantics but no reviewer-gated retry loop; retries are orchestrator judgment.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Retry-with-judgment is a runtime loop here; in CRX it is an emergent orchestrator behavior with no record.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: needs attempt records, a reviewer step, and a chooser rule in MissionRuntime.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: valuable for high-stakes missions where attempt selection beats last-attempt-wins, but adds reviewer cost to every retry.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Run a task with 3 attempts where attempt 2 is best; assert the chooser selects attempt 2's submission and that stats for the three attempts are recorded separately.

PROBLEM: Conversations need durable sessions that survive process restarts, with swappable backends from dev (in-memory) to prod (database).
MECHANISM: SessionService interface with create_session, get_session, and append_event; Session is a pydantic model holding the event list; backends include in-memory, SQLite, full database, and Vertex AI. Events are appended, never rewritten. Source: src/google/adk/sessions/base_session_service.py, session.py.
INVARIANT: append_event only appends; session identity (app/user/session ids) is stable across backend swaps.
FAILURE_MODEL: Backend write failure surfaces as an exception; in-memory backend loses everything on restart by design.
SECURITY_MODEL: Sessions contain full conversation history; backend access control is the security boundary, and there is none in the SDK itself.
SCALING_MODEL: Sessions partition by (app, user, session) ids; event lists grow unbounded per session.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX ping_events is the durable store but there is no session abstraction; ADK's backend-swappable session service is the shape CRX's session layer could take.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: ADK sessions are mutable containers with append-only events; CRX has the events but no container identity.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: introduce a session entity over ping_events with the same three-method interface; SQLite backend first.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: standardizes session handling, but CRX's event log already covers durability; the gain is the interface, not the storage.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Write a session to SQLite, restart the process, get_session and assert the event list is intact; swap to in-memory and assert the same code path works with restart-loss.

PROBLEM: Agent state mixes app-wide configuration, per-user data, and per-turn scratch; without namespaces, keys collide and user data leaks across users.
MECHANISM: State keys are namespaced by prefix: 'app:' for application-scoped state shared across users, 'user:' for per-user state. The prefix is part of the key, enforced by the State class. Source: src/google/adk/sessions/state.py.
INVARIANT: A key without a recognized prefix is temp/session-scoped; prefixed keys never collide across scopes even with identical suffixes.
FAILURE_MODEL: Code that reads a bare key when it meant a prefixed one silently gets the wrong scope's value; prefixes are convention enforced at the accessor, not at storage.
SECURITY_MODEL: Namespacing prevents accidental cross-user reads but is not an authorization boundary; the store still needs access control.
SCALING_MODEL: Zero runtime cost; purely a key convention.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has one authoritative owner per constitutional concern but no key-namespacing convention for scoped state.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Tiny mechanism, large blast radius: scope becomes visible in every key instead of living in documentation.
INTEGRATION_COST: Trivial: adopt the prefix convention in CRX state keys and enforce it in the state accessor.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: cheap prevention of an entire class of cross-scope leaks.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Write app:theme and user:theme, then read bare 'theme' and assert it does not return either; read user:theme as a different user id and assert the accessor refuses or returns empty.

PROBLEM: Common multi-agent topologies (pipeline, fan-out, retry-loop) get reimplemented ad hoc in every project with subtle ordering bugs.
MECHANISM: Composite shell agents with typed state: SequentialAgent runs sub-agents in order tracking current_sub_agent; ParallelAgent runs sub-agents concurrently on separate branches; LoopAgent repeats tracking current_sub_agent and times_looped. Each composite is itself an agent, so composites nest. Source: src/google/adk/agents/sequential_agent.py, parallel_agent.py, loop_agent.py.
INVARIANT: The composite's typed state always names the current sub-agent; a crashed composite can resume by reading current_sub_agent and times_looped.
FAILURE_MODEL: A failing sub-agent fails the composite unless the composite handles it; ParallelAgent branch failures need an explicit aggregation policy.
SECURITY_MODEL: Sub-agents run with their own tools; the composite does not sandbox them beyond what each agent already enforces.
SCALING_MODEL: ParallelAgent branches multiply context and cost; SequentialAgent is O(steps).
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has MissionRuntime and WorkerRuntime but no declarative composite topologies; sequencing is orchestrator code.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Topology as a typed, stateful object rather than as imperative orchestration code.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: model composites as mission step types with the same state fields; nesting falls out naturally.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: removes a class of ordering bugs, but only pays off once CRX has run identity and step state.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Build a SequentialAgent of two sub-agents, crash between them, and assert resume continues at the second; build a ParallelAgent and assert branches do not share mutable state.

PROBLEM: Workflow control signals (did the reply finish, was it interrupted, was there an error, is there structured output) get bolted onto messages as ad-hoc metadata that every consumer parses differently.
MECHANISM: Msg is a single typed envelope carrying both content and workflow-control fields: name, content blocks, role, id, metadata, created_at, usage, plus finished_at, finished_reason (error/interrupted/exceed_max_iters, set when a REPLY_END event is applied), and structured_output. Control state rides on the message itself, not in a side channel. Source: src/agentscope/message/_base.py.
INVARIANT: finished_reason is None until a REPLY_END event is applied; once set it is terminal and describes exactly how the reply ended.
FAILURE_MODEL: Consumers that read content without checking finished_reason can treat an interrupted reply as complete.
SECURITY_MODEL: The envelope carries usage and metadata that may include sensitive routing info; redaction must happen at the envelope level.
SCALING_MODEL: Envelope overhead is constant per message.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX worker results reify as canonical events but the envelope shape (what control fields ride along) is not standardized.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Control fields as first-class typed message fields rather than metadata-dict conventions.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: standardize the worker-result envelope with finished_reason-style terminal states.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: kills a family of 'was this reply actually finished' bugs.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Interrupt a reply mid-stream and assert finished_reason is 'interrupted' and finished_at is set; consume the message ignoring finished_reason and confirm the failure mode is observable.

PROBLEM: Agents burn unbounded money and time: nothing stops a runaway loop except the model's own judgment, which is exactly what fails in a loop.
MECHANISM: UsageLimits enforced by the runtime on every run: cost_limit (USD), request_limit (default 50, checked before each model request), tool_calls_limit, input/output/total token limits (checked after each response). RunContext is generic over a typed deps object, so tools receive type-checked dependencies. Source: pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/usage.py, _run_context.py.
INVARIANT: The request limit is checked before each request, so a run can never exceed request_limit model calls regardless of what the model wants.
FAILURE_MODEL: Hitting a limit raises instead of pausing, so a run killed at 50 requests loses its in-progress state unless the caller persists it; cost accounting depends on provider-reported prices.
SECURITY_MODEL: Limits are a budget control, not an authorization control; they bound damage but do not prevent a single malicious tool call.
SCALING_MODEL: Limit checks are O(1) counters per request.
CRX_ANALOG: No analog; CRX has no per-run budget enforcement. This is a missing safety rail for autonomous missions.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Budgets as runtime-enforced invariants rather than orchestrator intentions.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: add a limits struct to MissionRuntime, check before each model/tool call, raise typed limit-exceeded events.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High: the cheapest insurance against runaway autonomous missions; the default-50-requests shape is a sane starting point.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Set request_limit=3 on a task needing 10 requests; assert the run raises after exactly 3 model calls and emits a typed limit event, not a silent stop.

PROBLEM: Long-running workflows must survive worker crashes, deploys, and restarts without losing their place or re-executing completed side effects.
MECHANISM: Event-sourced durable execution: the workflow history is the source of truth, persisted by the Temporal server. On recovery, workflow code replays the history to reconstruct state; completed activities are not re-executed because their results are in the history. unsafe.is_replaying() and is_replaying_history_events() let workflow code branch during replay. Source: temporalio/workflow/_sandbox.py, _context.py.
INVARIANT: Workflow code must be deterministic: replaying the same history must produce the same decisions, or replay diverges and the workflow task fails.
FAILURE_MODEL: Nondeterministic workflow code (random, wall-clock, unguarded I/O) causes non-determinism errors on replay; workflow code changes need versioning or in-flight workflows break.
SECURITY_MODEL: The server holds all histories; worker compromise exposes only workflows the worker polls for, but history contains all inputs including secrets.
SCALING_MODEL: Production-proven at large scale; history size grows with workflow length and long histories slow replay.
CRX_ANALOG: Closest production analog to CRX's event-sourcing ambition: ping_events as history, MissionRuntime as the replayer. Temporal proves the model at scale.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Temporal separates deterministic workflow code (replayable) from activities (side effects, recorded); CRX has not yet drawn this boundary.
INTEGRATION_COST: High to adopt fully; low to adopt the core distinction: mark which mission code must be deterministic and replayable vs which parts are effectful activities.
EXPECTED_VALUE: High as a design reference: the workflow/activity split and the determinism invariant are the two ideas CRX most needs.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Write a workflow that calls datetime.now() unguarded, run it, kill the worker mid-run, and assert replay raises a non-determinism error; guard with is_replaying() and assert recovery succeeds without re-executing completed activities.

PROBLEM: Deterministic replay is unenforceable if workflow code can import anything and do I/O anywhere; developers will accidentally break replay.
MECHANISM: Workflow code executes in a sandbox with import restrictions and nondeterminism guards; unsafe.sandbox_unrestricted() is the explicit, auditable escape hatch for code that opts out, and SandboxImportNotificationPolicy controls how unexpected imports are handled. Source: temporalio/workflow/_sandbox.py.
INVARIANT: Code inside the sandbox cannot perform actions that would break deterministic replay; opting out requires calling an explicitly named unsafe API.
FAILURE_MODEL: Overuse of sandbox_unrestricted() silently reintroduces nondeterminism; the sandbox cannot catch every nondeterministic library.
SECURITY_MODEL: The sandbox is a determinism boundary, not a security boundary; it does not defend against malicious workflow code.
SCALING_MODEL: Sandbox import checks happen at workflow load; negligible per-run cost.
CRX_ANALOG: No analog; CRX has no determinism enforcement on mission code.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Makes the determinism requirement mechanically checkable instead of a documentation request.
INTEGRATION_COST: High: requires defining what CRX mission code may and may not do, plus sandbox infrastructure.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: the escape-hatch naming (unsafe.*) is the portable idea; full sandboxing is a large investment for CRX's current stage.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Import a banned module (e.g. socket) inside workflow code and assert the sandbox rejects it at load; wrap the same import in sandbox_unrestricted() and assert it loads, proving the boundary is explicit rather than absent.

PROBLEM: In multi-step processes, every step sees every event, so internal bookkeeping events leak to external consumers and steps cannot hide their coordination chatter.
MECHANISM: KernelProcessEvent carries a visibility flag: Internal events are only routed to steps within the same process, Public events are also visible outside the process to other processes or external systems. Steps emit via KernelProcessStepContext.emit_event with an explicit visibility. Source: python/semantic_kernel/processes/kernel_process/kernel_process_event.py, kernel_process_step_context.py.
INVARIANT: An Internal event never leaves its process boundary; visibility is set at emit time and cannot be upgraded by a receiving step.
FAILURE_MODEL: A step that needs an external signal but emits Internal will wait forever; mislabeled Public events leak internal coordination details to outside consumers.
SECURITY_MODEL: Visibility is a routing scoping, not encryption; a compromised step inside the process sees all Internal events.
SCALING_MODEL: Zero-cost routing filter; events are still constructed even when filtered.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has one authoritative owner per constitutional concern but no event visibility scoping; all ping_events are equally visible to all consumers.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Visibility is a first-class event field here; CRX would need it as a new event attribute plus routing rules.
INTEGRATION_COST: Low: add a visibility field to event envelopes and filter in projection/subscription paths.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: prevents internal coordination chatter from leaking into external projections and reduces consumer noise.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Emit an Internal event from a step in process A and subscribe from outside; assert it is never delivered. Emit the same payload as Public and assert delivery.

PROBLEM: Process steps need durable, typed state to resume after interruption, but untyped state dicts drift and break silently across code changes.
MECHANISM: KernelProcessStep is generic over TState; on activation the runtime calls activate(state: KernelProcessStepState[TState]), restoring the step's typed state. State shape is part of the step's type signature. Source: python/semantic_kernel/processes/kernel_process/kernel_process_step.py, kernel_process_step_state.py.
INVARIANT: A step's state always conforms to its declared TState type; activation with a mismatched state type fails at deserialization.
FAILURE_MODEL: Changing TState without migrating stored state breaks activation of in-flight processes; the runtime surfaces a deserialization error, not silent corruption.
SECURITY_MODEL: Step state may contain sensitive intermediate data; state stores need the same access control as the event log.
SCALING_MODEL: State is per step instance; serialization cost is per activation.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX WorkerRuntime results reify as events but intermediate worker state is not typed or restorable; no per-step state schema exists.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Typed state as part of the step's contract vs CRX's untyped intermediate state.
INTEGRATION_COST: Medium: define typed state schemas per mission step kind and an activate/restore path in the runtime.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: makes step state explicit and versionable, which is prerequisite for durable per-attempt run identity.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Persist a step's state, change TState incompatibly, and attempt activation; assert a deserialization error rather than silent wrong-typed state.

PROBLEM: In an agent loop mixing model inference and tool operations, two components can register the same tool name, causing ambiguous dispatch where the wrong tool executes.
MECHANISM: The agent loop is a typed StateMachine generic over session S and effects E; each Step is either an Operation (tool execution producing effects) or an Inference (model call). When operations register their tools into the inference input, duplicate tool names across operations are rejected hard with an error ('multiple operations registered tool'). Source: crates/goose-agent/src/machine.rs.
INVARIANT: Tool names are unique across all operations in the state machine; dispatch from a tool call to its operation is unambiguous by construction.
FAILURE_MODEL: A duplicate registration fails the whole machine build instead of silently shadowing; removing an operation at runtime requires rebuilding the machine.
SECURITY_MODEL: The uniqueness check prevents tool shadowing attacks where a later-registered malicious tool hijacks a trusted tool's name.
SCALING_MODEL: Registration check is O(tools) at build time; dispatch is a hash lookup.
CRX_ANALOG: CRX has no MCP/tool-execution path yet (known gap); when it gains one, tool-name collisions across providers will be a real risk.
SEMANTIC_DELTA: Collision rejection at machine-build time vs the usual runtime-first-registration-wins behavior.
INTEGRATION_COST: Trivial: when CRX builds its tool registry, reject duplicate tool names across providers at registration time.
EXPECTED_VALUE: Medium: cheap, prevents a real class of dispatch bugs and shadowing attacks in the future tool path.
FALSIFICATION_TEST: Register two operations exposing the same tool name; assert machine construction fails with the duplicate-tool error rather than dispatching to either.
